posts.title: Introducing »Relaxed« 1.0.0 for Zed
posts.description: The Relaxed theme is now available for Zed. Version 1.0.0 brings the calm colors you might have enjoyed in your terminal and VS Code to the blazingly fast, Rust-powered editor. Zed now feels like home 🕶️ Backstory Back in 2018 I released the »Relaxed Theme«, a color scheme I had fine-tuned for my terminal over quite a while. A Visual Studio Code version followed shortly after and has been used by me and many others for almost a decade. Today I’m happy to announce that »Relaxed Theme« has shipped as version 1.0.0 for Zed 🎉 How I ended up here I stumbled upon Zed a while ago and got curious. I played around a bit and began configuring it to my needs (pretty much in a VS Code style). After some basic settings, tossing panels from one side to the other and installing just one additional extension, I was quite taken with it. After scrolling through settings.json , some additional minor tweaks here and there and using Zed as my primary work tool, I became a fan. The built-in »One Dark« theme

posts.title: Stencil and Storybook – How to generate argTypes from JSDoc comments
posts.description: When using Stencil with Storybook, you’ll quickly notice that Controls don’t work out of the box. This guide shows you how to automatically generate proper argTypes from your JSDoc comments using the Custom Elements Manifest. The final result: a proper table with controls matching the props types. The Problem Storybook for Web Components relies on the Custom Elements Manifest to generate the props/attributes table below your default story from your JSDoc blocks. Even when using correct TypeScript types and JSDoc comments, these don’t automatically translate into proper Storybook Controls without some additional setup. You’ll end up with “Set object” buttons instead of proper select, radio, or boolean controls to play with your components attributes in Storybook. Let’s tackle this problem step by step. 1. posts.title: How to flash ESP8266 (and ESP32) to use Espruino firmware on macOS
posts.description: Espruino is a firmware with an integrated JavaScript interpreter for microcontrollers coming with it’s own IDE. So it’s possible to run JavaScript natively on the most affordable microcontrollers like the ESP8266. This Guide helps you to set things up to explore the possibilities of the Internet of Things using the language of the web. About Espruinos JavaScript abilities Espruino sports a subset of ES6 features as shown in the language feature list. You’ll find the comprehensive API documentation including built-in modules on the website as well. The module system is similiar to CommonJS but you won’t be able to use the npm eco system. Learn more about Espruinos modules . Espruino compatible microcontrollers Espruino sells different own development boards with various hardware features that are specifically designed to work with this firmware.
